messages.subject: Overestimation of copy number
messages.body_plain:
Dear Gavin,

I have recently started using TitanCNA for some noisy data. It seems to consistently over-estimate the copy number especially in regions where there is no change. So most commonly I see a copy number estimation of 3 where it should have been 2. ichorCNA however predicts the copy number correctly in those regions. So I think this might be because most of the noise is in the BAF data and the readCount data is fairly alright.

I was just wondering if there is  way to adjust for this? For instance if there is a parameter that increases the importance of ReadCounts over BAF? Or any other parameter that might be of any help for analysing noisy data?

Thanks a lot.
Best
Mo

messages.subject: Re: Overestimation of copy number
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mo,

Thank you for your interest in TITAN.

Without seeing some example plots of the data, it is hard for me to know is going on exactly.  However, there are a few ways, in general, to help prevent over-segmentation.
- Increase txnExpLen: This value is used to govern the transition probabilities. The higher this value is set, fewer segments will be generated.
- Increase minDepth: This value is used to help filter which SNPs are used for BAF. If your data is noisy, then it might be a coverage issue. This argument can help with that.
- Increase alphaK: This value is the hyper parameter for the Gaussian model (log ratio). If your data is very clean, then increasing this value will allow for better fitting of the model and also increase the probabilities contributed by the log ratio compared to the allelic ratio. This parameter change will likely give you the biggest improvement if the log ratio data is really clean.

You make a good point about weighting read coverage and allelic fraction (BAF) more directly. I have considered adding this into the model but never got around to it.

Hope this helps,

Gavin

messages.subject: Re: Overestimation of copy number
messages.body_plain:
Dear Gavin,

Thank you very much for your reply. I have already tried some of these parameters with not much luck. Attached you can see an example.

On the left is my control data with default parameters which returns very clean profiles. On the right is the corresponding noisy data. On the top right as you can see, despite the noise, ichorCNA correctly predicts the copy numbers, however when the data is passed on to Titan, it predicts too many segments. When I increase the txnExpLen parameter to 1e20 to reduce the segment numbers however, it decides to estimate a higher ploidy for the 6q segment. Any idea why this might be happening and if there might be a way to solve it?

Thanks again
Best
Mo

thank you for your work on TitanCNA. Please may I ask for a piece of advice :

would you recommend using (running) the algorithm per each chromosome individually, or on all chromosomes at the same time (on a genome-wide scale).

I am asking simply because multiple copies of a chromosome may potentially introduce biases when computing the diploid status of the genome. Thanks !

-- bogdan

messages.subject: Re: using TITANCNA per chromosome or on genome-wide scale
messages.subject_clean: using TITANCNA per chromosome or on genome-wide scale
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bogdan,

My recommendation is to run TitanCNA on the whole genome. Gains and losses of individual chromosomes are predicted as such and the ploidy of the genome is predicted as the average copy number genome-wide. The more complicated task of deciding the actual ploidy of your sample is probably what you are concerned with. For example, if the tumor ploidy estimate is 3.2, does this mean diploid with numerous chromosomal gains. This is more difficult to interpret.

Best,
Gavin

messages.subject: Re: about the S_Dbw validity index and the results
messages.subject_clean: about the S_Dbw validity index and the results
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bogdan,

Sorry for the delay and thanks for your patience.

The correct answer, based on your plots, should be numClusters=1.  The most important indication would be that the HET and NLOH segments in the same log ratios in chr4. Whereas in the numClusters=2, chr4, the HET and clonal NLOH have different log ratios.
However, TitanCNA does estimate its parameters by considering all chromosomes so there could be some stronger evidence of sub clonal events in other chromosomes.
It is very interesting that the S_Dbw are both so low that it picked the incorrect solution (assuming all other chromosomes also support 1 cluster).
This is why it is still very important to manually inspect the results, as you have been doing.

Hope this helps answer your question.
Best,
Gavin

messages.subject: Re: a question about CNV results
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bogdan,

Which version of TitanCNA are you using? In v1.7.2, I have included a check for clusters that contain very few data points (i.e. cluster=2 solution only have a few data points for Z1). See https://github.com/gavinha/TitanCNA/blob/master/NEWS for removeEmptyClusters()
Also, are you using a helper script for selecting your solutions? https://github.com/gavinha/TitanCNA/blob/master/scripts/R_scripts/selectSolution.R

Based on the plots, numClusters=1 appears to be more accurate. It is possible that there are other chromosomes that support sub clonal events (numClusters=2) but from chr12 alone, it seems 1 cluster is correct. It is good that you are manually inspecting your results.
The reason cluster=2 is incorrect in this plot is because it has overfitted to a sub clonal (Z2) cluster and therefore very few data points are in Z1. If all the chromosomes look like this, that is, all chromosomes have most data points in Z2 and not Z1, then removeEmptyClusters() should have corrected this solution. Of course, unless there is an abundance of noisy data in Z1 that avoids correction.

Best,
Gavin

messages.subject: Re: Overestimation of copy number
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mo,

Perhaps another way to account for noisy data is actually to decrease the alphaK argument from 10000 to 5000 or 1000. This is the hyper parameter for the variance parameter, which in term is used to model the variability of the log ratio data. Earlier, I had thought you said you had clean log ratios.  While the log ratio is cleaner than the BAF, it isn't as clean as your control sample.

See if this helps.

Best,
Gavin

messages.subject: Snakemake workflows for TitanCNA and 10X Genomics analysis
messages.subject_clean: Snakemake workflows for TitanCNA and 10X Genomics analysis
messages.body_plain:
Dear Users,

For those who wish to use a TitanCNA workflow that is relatively easy to set up and also allows for customization of parameter settings, I provide and maintain a Snakemake workflow that I use myself. The README includes instructions on how to set up and run the analysis as well as a description for the configuration.

https://github.com/gavinha/TitanCNA/tree/master/scripts/snakemake

Thank you to users who have reported bugs through GitHub. Please continue to post issues there and questions about interpretation, concepts, and discussions in this Google Groups.

10X Genomics WGS analysis
https://github.com/gavinha/TitanCNA_10X_snakemake
I have also built a Snakemake workflow for TitanCNA analysis of 10X Genomics WGS data. The specific features used in this pipeline are the use of
1. Molecule-based coverage (instead of read coverage)
2. Haplotype-based copy number which uses phasing information instead of allelic ratios from individual SNPs.
Note that LongRanger will need to be run first to generate barcode-aware aligned BAM files and variant/phasing called sites.

The methods are described in a recent publication (Methods section): https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29909985

Thank you for your interest in TITAN.

Best,
Gavin
